Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.

Negative Appraisals.value: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me
What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened

Fire/flames and snakes suggest trauma content not represented anywhere in the memory or appraisal items and not plausibly linked to partner physical abuse unless there were specific undisclosed trauma details. The rest of the profile centers on bodily pain, terror, injustice, contamination, and identity change following interpersonal assault, so these two triggers appear clinically incoherent with the formulation and with the other selected items.

vignette:
Kofi, a thirty-year-old curriculum designer, presented for therapy stating that he no longer recognized the man he saw in the mirror. For the past eight months, since the end of his relationship, he had felt a profound sense of being fundamentally altered, as if he were living in a stranger’s skin. The person he had become, he explained, was a ghost of the confident, engaged man he used to be, and this sense of alienation from himself was now unbearable. The change began the night his ex-partner, Marcus, came home smelling heavily of whiskey. An argument had started over something trivial, but it quickly soured when Marcus, his voice thick with contempt, made a cruel remark about Kofi’s family in Ghana. As the fight escalated, the pot of rice they were cooking began to burn on the stove, filling the small apartment with an acrid, choking smoke. It was in that moment, with the smell of alcohol on Marcus’s breath and the stench of burning food in the air, that the violence began.

In the months since, Kofi has found that the world is littered with reminders of that night. A few weeks ago, at a work happy hour, a colleague jostled past him, and the faint smell of beer on their clothes was enough to send him reeling. Instantly, he was no longer in the loud, cheerful bar but was back on his own kitchen floor. The memory was not a simple thought; it was a full-bodied assault. He could feel the phantom ache of a blossoming bruise on his ribs, a sharp, localized pain that mirrored the original injury precisely. The terror returned with the same suffocating intensity, a primal fear that left him breathless and disoriented in the middle of a crowd of his smiling coworkers.

These moments of re-experiencing leave a toxic residue. After the flashback at the bar faded, Kofi was left with a crushing wave of self-recrimination. The memory of his own helplessness reinforced a belief that had been taking root for months: that he was no longer the strong, capable person he once was. The vivid recall of the injustice—that Marcus had walked away without consequence while he was left with these invisible wounds—fed a simmering, powerless anger. More than anything, the memory of being physically overpowered left him with a feeling of being permanently soiled. He described it as a sense of contamination that clung to him, a dirtiness that no amount of showering could ever seem to wash away. This feeling has become a constant companion, tainting his interactions and his perception of himself.

The intrusive memories have also taught him what to fear, creating a vicious feedback loop. Because the flashbacks so often bring with them the scent of stale whiskey and burnt food, Kofi now finds himself in a state of constant olfactory vigilance. He will walk a different route to work to avoid passing a restaurant kitchen whose vents sometimes exhale the smell of charred food. At his office, where he designs educational programs, he avoids the staff room entirely after a coworker burns their toast, the smell sending a jolt of panic through him. This hypervigilance has made him seem distant and anxious to his colleagues, further cementing his belief that he has become unrecognisable.

Not every trigger needs to bring back the full memory to inflict damage. Last week, a well-meaning manager asked him about his family, a simple, friendly question about their well-being. The comment itself, so reminiscent of Marcus’s sneering words, was enough to make Kofi’s skin crawl. It didn’t precipitate a full flashback, but it instantly activated his deeply held conviction that he was contaminated, that this ugly secret was now somehow connected to the family he loved. He felt the unfairness of it all like a physical weight—the inability to have a normal, human conversation without this shadow falling over him. He made a curt excuse and fled to the men’s room, overwhelmed by a shame that felt both immense and irrational. It was after a video call with his sister, where he found himself unable to answer her questions and ended the call abruptly, that he finally sought help. He could no longer stand the person the trauma had made him, and he was terrified that if something didn’t change, he would lose himself completely.
